ch10 - Rounding Third and Heading Home.md
chapters.relation: Joe Kraus uses Gaston Bachelard's Poetics of Space to read baseball's 'home': the batter begins at home yet must leave it, face the pitcher's threat, and return to make scoring meaningful, which is Bachelard's dialectic of shelter versus threat (with Joseph Campbell's monomyth alongside). Freud's uncanny (unheimlich, un-home-like) explains why home plate is both inviting and demoralizing. Bachelard's 'well-determined centers of revery' and Benedict Anderson's shared-news account of nationhood then explain ballparks as communal homes, from Wrigleyville to 'Cardinal Nation' in Quincy, Illinois, and why the Dodgers leaving Brooklyn felt like losing a home.

chapters.file: ch11 - The Obligation to Play Baseball.md
chapters.relation: Horan and Solomon examine the 2001-02 contraction fight in which Judge Harry Crump ordered the Minnesota Twins to honor their Metrodome lease and play the 2002 season. They argue the Minnesota courts smuggled Bentham-Mill utilitarian reasoning about the public good into contract law, which normally awards only money damages, because baseball's antitrust exemption (from Justice Holmes's 1922 ruling through Justice Blackmun's 1972 opinion) had always treated the game as more than a business. Having long profited from special treatment, the owners lost when Bud Selig's plan to eliminate the Twins collided with the same 'greatest good for the greatest number' logic.

chapters.file: ch12 - Second Inning - You Gotta Believe!.md
ch13 - Who Should Be Committed.md
chapters.relation: Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.

chapters.file: ch14 - Kierkegaard Lays It Down.md
chapters.relation: Willie Young uses the sacrifice bunt (Derek Jeter's perfect one versus Placido Polanco's failed one) to test philosophical accounts of sacrifice. Aristotle treats bunting for teammates as friendship and civic virtue in the polis, while Seneca's Stoic sacrifices only to exercise virtue itself, detached from particular friends and refusing retaliation for hit batters. Hegel's modern ideal of self-renunciation makes the player a cog in the team machine (the Big Red Machine), obeying the manager's calculations; against this, Kierkegaard's Abraham, whose absolute duty to God is 'higher than the universal' through infinite resignation, exposes baseball's mechanical, manager-ordered sacrifice and asks whether the game trains obedient citizens who sacrifice as they are told.

chapters.file: ch15 - Third Inning - The Umpire’s New Clothes.md
ch16 - The Ambiguous Consolations of Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Ted Cohen shows that 'ties go to the runner' is no convention but follows from Rule 6.05(j) (the runner is out only if tagged before he touches first), then discovers that Rule 7.08(e) contradicts 6.05(j) once 6.09(a) makes a batter who hits a fair ball a runner: on a tie at first the rules say both out and safe. His letters to the National League rules committee get a polite brush-off ('there never are any ties'), and the essay meditates on how players barely know the rules (the 2000 World Series third-strike misplay, cricket's time-wasting law, the spitball rule's gaps) and how rules written 'by journeymen lawyers' charm yet fail. Philosophy's consolation is ambiguous: knowing the rules cost him his teammates' respect, who 'knew the game in some other way.'

chapters.file: ch17 - The Integrity of the Game.md
chapters.relation: J.S. Russell argues umpires have far more discretion than 'rules are all an umpire has to work with' allows. Via J.L. Austin's performative utterances, a call both creates the out and reports a witnessed event, so it can be false; hence unwitnessed or deceived calls (Ken Burkhart's 1970 World Series missed tag, phantom tags, Bernardo Carbo never touching the plate) should be reviewable to prevent an 'anti-game.' Via Ronald Dworkin's law-as-integrity he then defends Lee MacPhail's reinstatement of George Brett's pine-tar home run and umpire Wes Curry's 1887 interference ruling through a 'first principle of games adjudication': interpret rules to preserve the lusory goal and the excellences the game tests, as umpires' de facto strike-zone management has held league batting averages near .260 for a century.

chapters.file: ch18 - Fourth Inning - Fair or Foul.md
ch19 - Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater.md
chapters.relation: Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.

chapters.file: ch20 - Five Questions about Good Sportsmanship.md
chapters.relation: Mark Hamilton asks whether there is lying in baseball (riffing on Jimmy Dugan's 'There's no crying in baseball') and sorts plays of deception by their target. Kant's absolute duty of truthfulness proves too broad for the hidden ball trick, Omar Vizquel's decoys, and faking a tag to fool Manny Ramirez: Aquinas's taxonomy of officious, jocose, and mischievous lies (with Bonhoeffer's situational truth-telling) shows these are jocose falsehoods in an agreed artificial contest, not immoral lies. But deception aimed at umpires is mischievous and immoral, as when Barry Bonds sells a trapped ball as a catch or runners cut bases in the illegal double squeeze; his five questions conclude that tricking opponents is strategy while tricking the officials destroys character and sport.

chapters.file: ch21 - Fifth Inning - Baseball and America.md
ch22 - Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy.md
chapters.relation: Eric Bronson reads the brawling 1977-78 'Bronx Zoo' Yankees (Steinbrenner firing Billy Martin five times, Martin dragging Reggie Jackson off the field in Fenway, Jackson's dugout charge and defiant bunt) as an argument that dissent is good for democracy. Through Alexis de Tocqueville's warnings about majority conformity and democratic leveling (Nietzsche's herd mentality), he argues America needs gadflies like Socrates condemned by Athens for 'creating tension' and MLK's nonviolent troublemakers, while Adam Smith's invisible hand shows the Yankees' internal self-interest and conflict still produced championships, unlike the harmonious 1979 'We Are Family' Pirates. Dysfunctional discord, like free speech, keeps teams and democracies from going stagnant.

chapters.file: ch23 - America’s Game.md
chapters.relation: William Morgan answers Richard Rorty's charge that American pop culture breeds only militaristic chauvinism by pointing to baseball's moral self-story: played for love of the game (Whitman) rather than market value. Using MacIntyre's notion of a practice's internal goods, he argues baseball's excellences and fair play are shared, socially constructed goods that resist commodification; through Annette Baier's ethics of trust and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' (saving your wife because she is your wife), the home team extends familial trust into a public moral community. Hence the moral outrage of 'Say it ain't so, Joe' after the 1919 Black Sox scandal and 'Say It Ain't So Sammy' after Sosa's corked bat: fans demand that players justify themselves to the community whose common good the game embodies.

holes.name: Gaston Bachelard
holes.what: French philosopher whose The Poetics of Space treats the home as 'our first universe', analyzing intimate space through a dialectic of shelter and threat.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reading of home plate, ballparks, and fan communities runs on Bachelard's dialectic of home and his 'well-determined centers of revery'.

holes.name: The Uncanny (unheimlich)
holes.what: Freud's notion of the terrifying that leads back to the long-familiar: the un-home-like that haunts the home.
holes.why: Chapter 10 explains why home plate feels both welcoming and threatening by applying the uncanny to batting and to scoring 'safe at home'.

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: French theorist of sacrifice and language who defines sacrifice as an offering that creates Meaning for the Other and for the social group.
holes.why: Chapter 14 opens and structures its account of the sacrifice bunt on Kristeva's definition of sacrifice as a meaning-creating, community-forming offering.

holes.name: Constitutive Rules (rules that define a game)
holes.what: Rules (Searle's 'X counts as Y in context C') that create the very activity they govern, as the rules of a game do, rather than regulating a pre-existing practice.
holes.why: Chapter 16 turns on rules that constitute baseball (players do not know them, they contradict each other), and chapters 19-20 ask when breaking them is cheating rather than strategy.

holes.name: Ronald Dworkin
holes.what: Legal philosopher who held that law includes moral principles beyond its rules and that adjudication should interpret the practice in its best light ('law as integrity').
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses Dworkin's integrity to justify MacPhail's pine-tar ruling, umpire Curry's 1887 call, and principled umpire discretion in hard cases.

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Philosopher of language who analyzed performative utterances: uses of words (promising, 'I do', 'You're out') that bring facts into being.
holes.why: Chapter 17 analyzes umpire calls as performatives that also report witnessed events, which grounds when calls can be true or false and hence corrected.

holes.name: The Lusory Goal (Bernard Suits)
holes.what: Bernard Suits's account of games as attempting to win by overcoming voluntarily accepted obstacles (lusory goals) through limited means (lusory means).
holes.why: Chapter 17's 'first principle of games adjudication' is formulated in lusory-goal and lusory-means terms to decide hard umpiring cases.

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: French political thinker whose Democracy in America praised democratic equality while warning of majority tyranny and democratic leveling into conformity.
holes.why: Chapter 22's thesis that dissenting Yankees are good for democracy is argued almost entirely through Tocqueville's analysis of majority rule and conformity.

holes.name: Annette Baier
holes.what: Moral philosopher who argued that morality is grounded in trust and solidarity, modeled on a child's well-placed trust in her mother, rather than in abstract principles.
holes.why: Chapter 23 builds its account of baseball as a public moral community on Baier's claim that trust is where all our moral ladders begin.
